en: The vessels were human vessels;
the elder was a Brahmin named Keśavadāsa.
The first is the eldest son of the elder.
The second is the second son of the elder, named Madhyama.
The third is the youngest son of the elder.
Ghaṭotkaca: A Rākṣasa; the son of Hiḍimbā and Bhīmasena.
Bhīmasena: The middle son of Kuntī.
Female roles.
Brāhmaṇī—the wife of the old man;
Hiḍimbā—a rākṣasī, the wife of Bhīmasena.
A drama.
(At the end of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager enters.
Stage Manager: May that foot of Hari protect you—the foot that brings despair to the hearts of the wives of the asuras, and which is as dark as a blue water-lily or a polished sword-blade.
He who, having set out for the conquest of the three worlds, shone like a bridge of beryl across the ocean of the sky.
Thus I address the noble sirs. Ah! While I am intent on addressing you, what indeed is this sound that is heard? Pray, let me see.
(Behind the scenes) Oh, father! Who indeed is this?
Sūtradhāra: Very well, I understand.
Oh, from his pronunciation of the word "bhoḥ," he is undoubtedly a Brāhmaṇa;
yet he is being terrified by some suspicious person of evil intent. (2)
(Backstage again) Oh, father! Who indeed is this?

The Stage Manager: Ah, now I have understood clearly. This is surely the son of the middle Pāṇḍava, born from Hiḍimbā as his source; he is a Rākṣasa-fire who terrifies the Brahmin community with whom he has no enmity. Alas, what a pity! For here—
Surrounded by his deluded sons—both young and accompanied by their wives—he falls into a state of agitation like a cow whose calf has been terrified. || 3 ||
(They exit.
End of the prologue. Then enters a Brahmin accompanied by his three sons and wife, with Ghaṭotkaca following behind.
The Brāhmaṇa: Oh, who indeed is this?
With hair scattered by the rays of the young sun, his long, tawny eyes blazing with the knitting of his brows.
At the end of the age, the form of Hara appeared like a cloud accompanied by lightning and a rain-garland. || 4 ||
First: Oh, dear father! Who indeed is this?
His eyes resemble a pair of planets, his chest is broad and full, his hair is tawny like gold, and he is clothed in thick silk garments.
Having the hue of a mass of darkness, with white, protruding fangs, like a fresh cloud containing water, with the crescent moon vanishing within it.
(5) Second: Who is this, sir?
With fangs like the tusks of a young elephant, a nose shaped like a plough, and arms like the trunks of excellent elephants, he is the color of a dark cloud;
blazing like the offered oblation into the fire, he stands resplendent and terrifying like the wrath of Śaṅkara, the destroyer of the city of Tripura.
The Third: Oh, father! Who indeed is this that afflicts us?
He is the thunderbolt for the lords of mountains, the hawk among all birds, the lion among herds of deer—Death itself, embodied in human form. (7)
Brāhmaṇī: Noble sir, who is this that torments us?
Ghaṭotkaca: Ho, Brāhmaṇa! Stop, stop!
Why do you flee, you whose essence of fortitude has been destroyed by fear of me, and whose power is rendered useless for protecting your terrified wife and children?
Like a serpent accompanied by its mate, distressed as the fierce fire of its wrath is fanned by the wind from the outstretched wings of Garuḍa. || 8 ||
"O Brāhmaṇa! You must not go, you must not go!
The Elder: "Brāhmaṇī! Do not be afraid! Dear children, do not be afraid! For his voice is full of deliberation.
Ghaṭotkaca: "O sir! Alas!"
I know, O best of the twice-born, that you are always and everywhere the most worthy of honor on earth;
yet this deed which must now be done by me is an improper one.
Having removed the mother's suspicion by means of his command. || 9 ||

The Old Man: O Brahmin lady! Do you not remember what was said by that venerable sage whose feet were moistened by water: "This forest is haunted by Rākṣasas; one must pass through it with vigilance"? That very thing has now produced fear.
The Brahmin Lady: Why does my noble husband appear as if his complexion has turned pale? The Old Man: What can I do, unfortunate as I am?
Brāhmaṇī: Surely we shall cry out!
First: Lady, to whom shall we cry out?
For this place is empty, its paths to the cardinal directions blocked by mountain ranges that shine like a mass of darkness.
The interior of the forest was crowded with birds and deer, and it was a dwelling desired by the wise.

The Old Man: O Brahmin lady! Do not fear, do not fear! Having heard that this is a place fit for the residence of noble-minded people, my terror has almost vanished. I suspect that the hermitage of the Pāṇḍavas must be not very far away;
for the Pāṇḍavas are lovers of battle and are compassionate toward those who seek their protection.
They take the side of the wretched and act with reckless violence;
they are capable of inflicting appropriate punishment here upon those whose appearance and conduct are so terrifying.
First: O father! I do not think there are Pāṇḍavas here.
Old Man: How do you know?
First: I heard from a certain Brāhmaṇa who was passing by that they have gone to the hermitage of the great seer Dhaumya to witness the sacrifice named Śata-kumbha.
The Elder: Alas, we are undone!
The First: Father, not all of them. It is said that the middle one was stationed here for the purpose of protecting the hermitage.
The Elder: If that is so, then all the Pāṇḍavas are present here.
First: And it is heard that at this very hour he is in a distant land for the sake of practicing his physical exercises.
Vṛddha: Alas, we are now without hope! Very well, my son; I shall take refuge in him for a moment.
First: Enough, enough with this exertion!
The Old Man: My son! A request is indeed the adversary of despondency. Very well, let us see. Ho there, man! Is there liberation for us?
Ghaṭotkaca: There is liberation, provided there is an agreement. The Old Man: What is the agreement?

Ghaṭotkaca said: "I have a venerable mother. She commanded me: 'Son, for the sake of breaking my fast, you must capture and bring some human being from this forest region. It was then that I found you.
You desire liberation along with your wife of virtuous conduct and your two sons;
yet, having discerned the relative strength of the situation, release one son."
The Elder: O you wretched Rākṣasa! Am I not a Brāhmaṇa?
How could I, a learned and aged Brāhmaṇa, find peace after giving my son, who is endowed with virtuous character, to this man-eater? || 13 ||
Ghaṭotkaca said: "O best of the twice-born, if you release even one son when requested, you shall meet with destruction along with your entire family in an instant. (14)
The Elder: This indeed is my firm resolve.
My body, worn out by old age, has fulfilled its purpose;
seeking my son, I shall offer it, consecrated by the rites, as an oblation into the fire of the Rākṣasa. (15)

Brāhmaṇī: Noble sir! Do not say such things. A woman who has as her sole duty her husband is called a "faithful wife" (*pativratā*). With this body, which has already yielded its fruit, I wish to protect both my noble husband and our family. Ghaṭotkaca: Lady! Surely it is not women that are desired by your honor?
The Old Man: I shall follow you.
Ghaṭotkaca: Ah! You are an old man; get out of the way!
The First: O father! I am indeed saying something to you.
The Elder: Speak, speak quickly!
The First: With my own life, I wish to protect the life of my preceptor.
For the sake of protecting this lineage, you ought to release me. (16)
The second said: "Noble sir! Do not say such a thing.
You are the eldest, the most excellent in the family and in the world, and very dear to our ancestors. Therefore, I myself shall go, following the conduct due to a teacher. (17)9
The third [brother] said: "Noble sirs! Do not say such a thing.
The elders have declared that an elder brother is equal to a father;
therefore, it is I who am worthy to effect the preservation of my gurus' lives. (18)
The first [brother] said: "Child! Do not say such a thing!
For when a father has fallen into calamity, he is rescued by the eldest son;
therefore, I myself shall go for the sake of protecting my elders' lives. (19)

Vṛddha: I cannot bear to abandon my eldest son, who is most dear to me. Brahmaṇī: As the noble sir desires the eldest, so do I desire the youngest. Second: If he is disliked by his parents, who now would find him pleasing?
Ghaṭotkaca: I am pleased. Come quickly!
Second: I am blessed that the life of my preceptor has been protected by my own life. For while affection for one’s kinsmen is great, affection for one’s body is indeed rare. (20)
Ghaṭotkaca: Oh, what paternal affection this young Brahmin has for his own kin!
Second: O father! I salute you. Old Man: Come, come, my son!
O you who are devoted to your guru, having bartered your own life for the life of your teacher,
attain the world of Brahmā, which is difficult to reach for those of undisciplined self.
Ghaṭotkaca: The young Brahmin is indeed taking his time. My mother’s mealtime is passing by. What indeed shall I do? Very well, I have seen it. O Brahmin! Let your son be summoned.
Vṛddha: Ah! Your speech is truly too demonic.
Ghaṭotkaca: Why are you angry? Please forgive me, please forgive me. This is a defect of my nature. Now, what is the name of your son?
The Elder: Even this cannot be heard.
Ghaṭotkaca: It is fitting, sir! O young Brahmin, what is your brother’s name?
The First: The ascetic Madhyama.
Ghaṭotkaca: "The Middle One"—this is fitting for him. I myself shall challenge him. Ho, Middle One! Middle One! Come quickly!
(Then Bhīmasena enters.
Bhīma: Ho! Whose voice is this?
In this forest, dense with trees and thick with peril, where hundreds of birds cry out, this sharp sound resounds loudly;
it stirs a fever in the heart.
For he is very much like Dhanañjaya in voice. || 25 ||

Ghaṭotkaca: The young Brahmin is indeed taking a long time. My mother’s mealtime is passing by. What indeed shall I do? Very well, I have an idea. I shall call out loudly: "O Madhyama! Come quickly! Bhīma: Ho there! Who is this in the middle of this forest who, having caused an obstacle to my exercise, calls me "Madhyama"? Very well, let me see. (Walking about and looking with astonishment) Oh, what a handsome man this is! For he— (Verse 10)
He has the face of a lion, the fangs of a lion, eyes like honey, and a smooth, deep voice; his eyebrows are tawny, his nose is like that of a hawk, and his jaw is like that of a lordly elephant;
his hair is radiant and well-knit; he has broad shoulders, a waist like a thunderbolt, the gait of an elephant and a bull, and long, thick-set arms.
It is evident that he is the son of a world-hero, born of a Rākṣasa woman and endowed with immense strength. || 26 ||
Ghaṭotkaca: The young Brahmin is indeed taking his time. I shall call out loudly. Ho there, Madhyama! Come quickly!
Bhīma: Ho there! Here I am.
Ghaṭotkaca: This is certainly not the young Brahmin. Oh, what a handsome man this is! He who is here—
Having the form of a lion, with arms equal to golden palm trees, slender-waisted, with wings smeared like those of Garuḍa,
Viṣṇu has eyes like the petals of a blooming lotus.
This one who has come like a kinsman steals away my eyes. || 27 ||
"O Madhyama! Indeed, I am summoning you.
Bhīma: "That is precisely why I have arrived.
Ghaṭotkaca: "Are you also a Madhyama?"
Bhīma: Not another [is the middle one].
I am the middle among those who are not to be slain and among the arrogant;
I am the middle on earth, O blessed one, and even the middle among my brothers. (28)
Ghaṭotkaca: It must be so.
Bhīma: Moreover, he is the middle one among the five elements, and the middle one among the kings of the earth.
In times of fear, he is mediocre in the world; in all undertakings, he is mediocre. || 29 ||
The Elder said: "Since 'the middle one' was mentioned by everyone, it must certainly be the middle Pāṇḍava;
out of pride, he has come here to rescue us, as if rising up from death itself. (30)

(Entering) The Middle One: Having sipped water here from this lotus pond—water as brilliant as a lotus petal, which is difficult to obtain in other worlds—I have offered it to myself by my own self. (31)
"O man! I am Ghaṭotkaca. "Now you have indeed reached the middle [age], O middle one! This way, this way!
The Old Man—(approaching Bhīmasena): "O middle one! Save the community of Brahmins!"
Bhīma: Do not fear, do not fear! I am Bhīma; I salute you, O elder. The Elder: May you live as long as the wind!
Bhīma: I am favored by your blessing. From what source could there be any fear for your honor?

The Elder: Listen. I am indeed a Brāhmaṇa named Keśavadāsa, belonging to the Māṭhara gotra and serving as an Adhvaryu priest according to the Kalpa branch [of the Yajurveda], residing in Yūpagrāma in Kurujāṅgala, which was formerly presided over by Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of the Kurus.

To my north lives my maternal uncle, named Yajñabandhu, belonging to the Kauśika gotra, in the village of Udyāmakagrāma. Accompanied by my wife, I have set out for the sake of his son’s initiation ceremony (upanayana).
Bhīma: May your path be free from harm! And what happened next? What happened next?

The Elder: Then this Rākṣasa, whose body is like a water-laden cloud, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, who moves with the playful gait of a lion, and who has protruding fangs— [approached me].
O, behold! Free from fear in this world, he approaches with the intent to kill you, along with your sons and attendants, in the very presence of those such as yourself. || 32 ||
Bhīma: So be it! This man has created an obstacle on the path for the Brahmins. Very well, I shall punish him. Ho there, man! Stop, stop!
Ghaṭotkaca: Here I am, standing still.
Bhīma: Why do you offend the Brahmins?
You have arisen like Rāhu over the aged Vipracandra, who is strewn with the constellations of his sons and possesses the lovely luster of his wife.
Ghaṭotkaca: Indeed so; he is Rāhu himself.
Bhīma: Ah!
This man has ceased all worldly activity, along with his wife and sons.
"Since he is not to be slain for any offense whatsoever, let this best of the twice-born be released."
Ghaṭotkaca: He is not released.
Bhīma: (To himself) Oh! Whose son must this man be?
Who, pray, is this thief of virtues among all my brothers?
Having seen this very same childish arrogance of the son of Subhadrā, I remember it now.
Ghaṭotkaca said: "He shall not be released.
Even if my father were to say with confidence, 'Let him be released,' he would still not be released; for he has been seized by the command of his mother. (36)
Bhīma—(To himself) How can it be "my mother’s command"? Oh, how this ascetic is devoted to the service of his elders!
Indeed, the mother is the deity of both men and deities;
it is by honoring our mother’s command that we have come to this state. (37)
(Aloud) O man! There is indeed something that must be asked.
Ghaṭotkaca—Speak, speak quickly!
Bhīma—What is the name of your mother?
Ghaṭotkaca: Listen; there was a Rākṣasī named Hiḍimbā, who was protected by the high-souled Pāṇḍava, the lamp of the Kuru lineage—she, the illustrious one, like the sky made full by the moon. (38)
Bhīma—(With joy, to himself) Indeed, this is the son of Hiḍimbā; his pride is truly worthy of him. His form, character, and strength are all greatly like those of his fathers.
But what kind of heart must he have, devoid of compassion toward living beings?
(Aloud) O man! Let him go!
Ghaṭotkaca: He shall not be released! Bhīma: O Brahmin! Take back your son; we shall follow after him.
The second said: "Do not say so!
My life-breaths were already surrendered long ago in preference for the life-breaths of my guru.
You, a youth endowed with beauty and virtue, should remain on this earth. (40)
Bhīma: Noble sir! Do not say such things. I am born of a Kṣatriya lineage, and Brāhmaṇas are indeed most worthy of honor. Therefore, I wish to exchange my body for the body of a Brāhmaṇa.
Ghaṭotkaca: Such is this Kṣatriya; that is why he is so arrogant. Very well, I shall kill him and take him away. Now, who has stopped him?
Bhīma: By me.
Ghaṭotkaca: Was it by you?
Bhīma: Indeed so. Ghaṭotkaca: In that case, you yourself should come.
Bhīma: Because he possesses such exceeding strength and heroism, I cannot follow him. If you have the power, lead me away by force.
Ghaṭotkaca: Do you recognize me?
Bhīma: I know you as my son.
Ghaṭotkaca: How? How am I your son?
Bhīma: Why do you become angry? May you forgive me. All subjects are addressed by the word "son" of the Kṣatriyas. It was for this reason that I spoke thus.
Ghaṭotkaca: You have taken up arms against those who are afraid.
Bhīma: I swear by the truth that I know no fear;
therefore, I wish to learn about it in your presence.
O good sir, tell me, what is its form?
Knowing virtue and vice, I shall obtain one who is my equal. || 41 ||
Ghaṭotkaca: Here, I shall teach you fear; take up a weapon.
Bhīma: A weapon? Here it is, taken up. Ghaṭotkaca: How so?
Bhīma: This right arm of mine, resembling a golden pillar and ever intent on subduing enemies, is my innate weapon. (42)
Ghaṭotkaca: This is worthy of my father Bhīmasena.
Bhīma: Now, who is this so-called Bhīma?
Is he Viśvakartā, Śiva, Kṛṣṇa, Śakra, Śaktidhara, or Yama?
"Among these, O gentle one, tell me: who is your father's equal?"
Ghaṭotkaca:—All [of you]!
Bhīma:—Fie upon this lie!

Ghaṭotkaca:—How? How can he say it is a lie? You insult my elder! Very well, I shall uproot this thick tree and strike you with it. (Having uprooted it, he strikes. Why, even with this he cannot be struck down? What indeed is the cause?
"I shall do it! Very well, I have seen it. Having uprooted this mountain peak, I shall strike him.
The mountain peak hurled by me will depart, taking his life with it.
Bhīma: "Even when enraged, a wild elephant in the forest would not attack a tiger."
Ghaṭotkaca:—(Striking) How is it that he cannot even be slain by me? What indeed shall I not do? Very well, I have seen enough!
Am I not the son of Bhīmasena and the grandson of the Wind-god?
Stand now, well-prepared for combat; there is no one equal to me in hand-to-hand wrestling.
(Thus both engage in hand-to-hand combat.
Ghaṭotkaca—(Having bound Bhīmasena:
How can you depart from here, having overstepped the prowess of my arms? Like an elephant oppressed by firm snares, you are tormented by my two arms.

Bhīma—(To himself) How have I been captured by him? O Suyodhana! Your enemy’s faction is growing; take care of your own protection. (Aloud) Ho there, man! Be on your guard! Ghaṭotkaca—I am on my guard. Bhīma—(Shaking off the wrestling hold)
Cast away your pride in your strength; O hero, you have seen my true essence!
Indeed, I feel no fatigue in hand-to-hand combat.

Ghaṭotkaca: How is it that he cannot even be killed by this? What indeed shall I do? Very well, I have found a way. I possess a magic noose obtained from my mother’s palace. Having bound him with that, I will take him away. Where indeed is water? O Mountain! Water, please! Ah, it flows! (Having sipped water, he mutters a mantra. O man!
Bound by the magic noose, you shall follow me at my command.
You shine, bound by ropes like the banner of Indra during a festival. || 47 ||

Bhīma: How am I bound by the noose of *māyā*? What shall I do now? Very well, I have found a way. By the grace of Maheśvara, I possess a mantra that grants liberation from the noose of *māyā*. I shall recite it. Where indeed can I find water? O young Brahmin! Bring the water contained in your water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
Old Man: Here is the water.
(Bhīma takes [the noose], sips water, mutters a mantra, and removes the illusion.
Ghaṭotkaca: Ah! The snare has fallen away. What shall I do now? Very well, I see. O man! Remember our previous agreement. Bhīma: "The agreement"? Yes, I remember it. Go ahead. (Both walk about.)
The Elder: My sons, what shall we do? Here goes Vṛkodara!

Having assailed this Rākṣasa, who possesses a blazing and fierce form and is endowed with the quality of fierce strength in his arms, he proceeds slowly, having shaken him off with ease, like a bull playfully shaking off a heavy downpour of rain.
Ghaṭotkaca: Stay here; I shall inform my mother of your arrival.
Bhīma: Very well; go.
Ghaṭotkaca: (Approaching) Mother! I salute you. This human being, whom you have long desired for food, has been brought here.
(Entering) Hiḍimbā: My son! Live long! (Jāta! Ciraṃ jīva!
Ghaṭotkaca: I am favored by you.
Hiḍimbā: My son, what kind of man was brought?
Ghaṭotkaca: Mother, he is a man only in appearance, not in valor.
Hiḍimbā: Is he a Brāhmaṇa?
Ghaṭotkaca: He is not a Brahmin. Hiḍimbā: Or is he an elder? (Or rather, a venerable one? Ghaṭotkaca: He is not an old man.
Hiḍimbā: Is he a child?
Ghaṭotkaca: He is not a child.
Hiḍimbā: If that is so, I shall see him for myself. (Both walk about. (If that is so, I shall see him for myself.)
Hiḍimbā: Has this human being been brought here?
Ghaṭotkaca: Mother, who is this?
Hiḍimbā: A madman is indeed our deity.
Ghaṭotkaca: Ah! Whose deity are you? Hiḍimbā: Yours and mine as well. (Yours and mine.
Ghaṭotkaca: What is the proof?
Hiḍimbā: This is the proof! Victory to my noble husband! (This is the proof! May my noble husband be victorious!
Bhīma: (Looking) But who is this? Ah, it is Queen Hiḍimbā!
While we were wandering in the dense forest, deprived of our kingdom...
O Goddess, by your spontaneous compassion, my torment has been destroyed! || 49 ||
"Hiḍimbā! What is this?
Hiḍimbā—(Into his ear) "Noble Lord! It seems like this.
Bhīma: She is a Rākṣasī by birth, not by her conduct.
Hiḍimbā: O madman! Pay homage to your father.
Ghaṭotkaca: O dear father!
It was because of ignorance that I did not previously pay you homage.
"You ought to show favor regarding this offense of your son."
"I am that Ghaṭotkaca, the forest fire for the Dhārtarāṣṭra forest; I offer my salutations. You ought to forgive your son’s rashness.

Bhīma: "Come, come, my son! Your transgression is already forgiven. (Embracing him) This is that very one who was the forest fire for the Dhārtarāṣṭra forest. Indeed, a father's heart is ever intent upon his son. My son, may you possess exceeding strength and prowess.
Ghaṭotkaca: "I am favored by your grace. 15.
The Elder: Thus is this Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīmasena.
Bhīma: My son, salute the venerable Keśavadāsa.
Ghaṭotkaca: Venerable sir, I salute you.
The Elder: May you possess fame for virtues equal to those of your father.
Ghaṭotkaca: I am favored.
The Elder: O Vṛkodara! Our lineage has been protected, and your own family has been uplifted. We shall now depart.
Bhīma said: "Through your favor, all this has become auspicious for us.
Our hermitage is not far away; let us go there after resting. (51)
The Old Man: Hospitality has been shown by him through this gift of life; therefore, let us depart for now.
Bhīma: May you go with your family for the sake of seeing one another again.
The Old Man: Very well; that is the primary course of action.
Bhīma: Hiḍimbā! This way, please. Dear Ghaṭotkaca! This way, please. We shall pay our respects even at the mere gateway of the hermitage of the venerable Keśavadāsa.
Just as the ocean is the source of rivers, and just as the sacrificial fire is the source of oblations.
Just as the mind is the source of the senses, so too is the Lord Upendra our master. || 52 ||
(All exit.
The drama titled *Madhyamavyāyoga* is completed.
